newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania miners denounce accord, continue strike.
newsitem.headline: Romania miners denounce accord, continue strike.

text.p: Coal miners in the impoverished Jiu Valley rejected a negotiated pay settlement on Wednesday and vowed to press on with a week-old strike.
"We will fight, we will not give up!" 4,000 miners chanted outside coal board offices in the mining centre of Petrosani.
Senior trade unionist Romeo Beja publicly tore up an accord he and other negotiators had signed overnight with government officials in Bucharest.
"I will follow you to the bitter end," he told the cheering crowd. "Look what I'm doing to this agreement."

Some protesters called for Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's reformist government to step down -- the first such appeal by workers since the centrists ousted the ex-communists in elections last November.
In neighbouring Ukraine, thousands of coal miners were also on strike demanding months of unpaid wages. Like their Romanian colleagues, they face closure of loss-making mines.

The Jiu Valley's 45,000 miners, the country's most militant, launched their strike demanding a 45 percent wage increase and guarantees against job cuts outlined in the centrist government's market reform programme.
Miners from adjacent districts attended the rally to offer support. But Romanian media said pits in other regions were operating normally after brief sympathy strikes.

Thousands of Jiu Valley miners rampaged through Bucharest twice in the early 1990s. They beat up anti-communist protesters in 1990 and attacked government offices a year later when the first post-communist government fell. Seven people were killed.
Miners' head Miron Cosma is on trial charged with leading the 1991 riots in the capital. A court this week rejected his appeal to be released during the proceedings.
Romanian authorities halted trains to the region for a time on Tuesday, but restored services after receiving pledges miners would not advance on Bucharest.
Trade union leaders said they were having difficulty containing rank-and-file fury. Beja urged strikers to stay in the region and to refrain from drinking or using "dirty language".
"Rejecting the compromise has brought the situation back to square one," one negotiator told Reuters. "I don't know what these guys will do. Let's hope it doesn't get out of control."
Ciorbea's government has pledged to restructure oversized and loss-making industries, including the mining sector.

The government has rejected miners' pay claims, citing budget restraints under its Western-backed reforms. It says planned tax cuts would provide the equivalent of a 15 percent pay increase from August.
Miners take home nearly twice the average Romanian wages equivalent to $80, and still have communist-era benefits like bonuses, cheap electricity and rent.
But many said they lived and worked in intolerable conditions.
"We have two taps for 40 families and a hole in the ground as a toilet," said Remus Caldararu.
His colleague, who identified himself as Serban, said much of the work in the pits was still manual.
"There are places where you work on your knees, strip down in the 40 degree (104 Fahrenheit) temperatures and cut coal with a shovel," he said. "How can you say we are overpaid?"
